result.summary: Apollodorus traces the descendants of Aeolus: Athamas and the golden fleece, Sisyphus, Salmoneus, Tyro and her sons, and Melampus. The chapter then turns to Jason, the building of the Argo, the voyage to Colchis and back with Medea, and the deaths of Pelias and Glauce and Medea's flight.

scenes.title: Athamas, Ino and the Ram
scenes.summary: Ino's plot against Phrixus and Helle leads Nephele to send them off on the golden ram. Helle drowns, Phrixus reaches Colchis, and Athamas, maddened, loses Ino's sons and settles elsewhere.
scenes.stakes: Phrixus faces sacrifice at the altar; Athamas loses his children and his home.

scenes.title: Sisyphus, Deion, Perieres, Salmoneus
scenes.summary: Brief genealogies of Sisyphus, Deion, Perieres and Magnes, and the punishments of Sisyphus and of Salmoneus, who impersonated Zeus.
scenes.stakes: Sisyphus and Salmoneus face punishment from Zeus for betrayal and impiety.

scenes.title: Tyro, Pelias, Neleus, Melampus
scenes.summary: Tyro bears twins to Poseidon; Pelias and Neleus grow up, kill Sidero and part ways. Neleus's sons die at the hands of Hercules except Nestor, and Melampus gains prophetic hearing.
scenes.stakes: Neleus's sons face death when Hercules ravages Pylus.

scenes.title: Melampus and the Kine; Admetus
scenes.summary: Melampus steals the kine of Phylacus for Bias to win Pero, and cures Iphiclus. Genealogies follow, then Apollo helps Admetus win Alcestis, who dies in his place and is sent back up.
scenes.stakes: Melampus is imprisoned and would be killed when the cell collapses; Admetus faces death.

scenes.title: Jason and the Building of Argo
scenes.summary: Pelias, warned of a man with one sandal, sends Jason for the Golden Fleece. Argus builds the Argo and many heroes assemble.
scenes.stakes: Jason risks his life on the quest; Pelias fears losing his kingdom.

scenes.title: Lemnos, Doliones and Hylas
scenes.summary: The Argonauts lie with the Lemnian women, accidentally kill King Cyzicus, and lose Hercules and Polyphemus in Mysia. Rival traditions on Hercules are noted.
scenes.stakes: The Argonauts risk night battle with friends; Hylas is taken by nymphs.

scenes.title: Amycus, Phineus, Clashing Rocks
scenes.summary: Pollux kills Amycus in boxing. At Salmydessus the Argonauts free Phineus from the Harpies, and following his advice pass the Clashing Rocks with a dove.
scenes.stakes: The Argonauts risk being crushed by the Clashing Rocks; Phineus is starved by the Harpies.

place.name: Salmydessus
place.modern_name: Black Sea coast of Thrace, Turkey

scenes.title: Colchis and the Fleece
scenes.summary: Aeetes sets Jason impossible tasks. With Medea's drugs Jason yokes the bulls, defeats the sown men, and takes the fleece, fleeing with Medea and Apsyrtus.
scenes.stakes: Jason risks death by fire-breathing bulls and Aeetes' treachery.

scenes.title: The Voyage Home
scenes.summary: Medea kills Apsyrtus; Zeus sends storms until Circe purifies the crew. They pass the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, the Phaeacians, and Talos, and reach Iolcus.
scenes.stakes: The wrath of Zeus and many sea perils threaten the crew; Medea may be returned to her father.

scenes.title: Pelias's Death and Medea's Fate
scenes.summary: Pelias kills Aeson's family; Medea tricks his daughters into boiling him. In Corinth Jason abandons Medea, who kills Glauce and her own children and flees to Athens, then Colchis.
scenes.stakes: Jason and Medea face exile and ruin; Glauce and the children are killed.

alias_notes.explanation: This translation uses the Greek name Zeus; Jove is its Roman equivalent.
Title for Artemis' counterpart is in the text; here it stands for Persephone, who sent Alcestis back up.

notable_quotes.reason: Jason's chance answer sends him after the Golden Fleece, launching the Argonaut quest.
Salmoneus imitates thunder and lightning, a classic image of impiety.

analysis.text: The chapter links genealogies to the Argonaut story, showing how family rivalry, broken oaths and divine anger drive fate.
Apollodorus compiles variant traditions, citing authors like Herodorus, Pherecydes and Apollonius, preserving lost mythographic sources.

legacy.text: The Argonaut myth inspired Apollonius's Argonautica and Euripides's Medea, shaping later literature.
The labor of Sisyphus gave rise to the phrase 'Sisyphean task'.

fun_facts.text: The chapter preserves rival accounts, including that Hercules never sailed on the Argo, showing how fluid the myth was.

language_notes.text: To "parch" the wheat is to roast the seed grain so it cannot sprout; the women did this secretly.
"Dearth" means scarcity or famine.
"Foretold" means the oracle supposedly declared this; Ino bribed or persuaded the messengers to report a false response.
Hellespont means "sea of Helle"; it is the modern Dardanelles strait. The story explains the name.
Zeus the god of Escape (Phyxios) fits Phrixus's rescue from sacrifice. "Grove of Ares" is a sacred wood of the war god.
"To wit" is an archaic phrase meaning "namely".
"Entertained by wild beasts" means given a meal as guests; the wolves' abandoned prey fulfils the oracle.
"Push it as he will" means however hard he pushes; the stone always rolls back down before reaching the top.
Dawn (Eos) was a goddess who often carried off handsome mortal men as lovers.
"To wit" is an archaic legal phrase meaning "that is to say," introducing the list of sons.
"Lightened" here means produced lightning; "kettles" are bronze cooking pots dragged to imitate thunder's noise.
"Hie" means hurry or go quickly; "plaint" is a complaint or lament. Both are archaic words in Frazer's translation.
"Lay with her" means had sexual intercourse; the god disguised himself as the river so she would not know him.
"Exposed" means abandoned outdoors to die or be found, a common ancient way of disposing of unwanted infants.
Pelias' name is explained from Greek pelios, "livid"; the translator's parenthesis "pelion" gives the root of the name.
"Contumely" means insulting, scornful treatment. Pelias' killing of Sidero at Hera's altar was sacrilege, so Hera was offended.
"To wit" means "that is to say"; it introduces the list of children.
"Purged his ears" means cleansed them; the snakes' licking gives Melampus the power to understand animal speech.
"Taking the auspices" means divining the future by observing birds and their flight; a "soothsayer" is a seer.
"Kine" is an archaic plural for cattle; the cows of Phylacus are the prize.
"Foretold" refers to Melampus's gift of prophecy; he knows beforehand he will be caught and imprisoned.
A soothsayer is a seer who foretells events or reads hidden truths.
"Gelding rams" means castrating them. The bloody knife frightened the child, causing the cause of Iphiclus's childlessness, which the vulture reveals.
"Beget" means to father a child; the rust drunk in a potion is the cure.
"Thrall" means slave or bondservant; Apollo served Admetus as punishment.
A "car" here means a chariot.
"The Maiden" is Persephone (Proserpine), queen of the dead, who sent Alcestis back up; the alternative version has Hercules rescuing her from Hades.
The oracle is the god's prophetic response, here from Delphi's Apollo; a man missing one sandal would be the threat to Pelias's rule.
"Apprehended" here means grasped or understood, not arrested.
"Husbandry" means farming; "abode" is an archaic past tense of abide, meaning stayed or lived.
Medea, later Jason's wife, will bring about Pelias's death; Hera's anger at Pelias is the reason given for Jason's fateful answer.
Dodona was an ancient oracle of Zeus in Epirus, famed for its sacred oak, so the ship's prow can prophesy.
"Admiral" here means the commander of the ship's expedition; Jason leads the voyage of the Argo.
"Bereft of men" means deprived of men; the island had none left.
"Noisome" means foul-smelling or harmful; Aphrodite punished the women with a stench.
The Pelasgians were a name for early, pre-Greek peoples of the Aegean lands; here they are the Doliones' habitual enemies.
"Minion" means favorite or beloved companion; Hylas was Hercules' young attendant and beloved. "Ravished" means carried off.
The Argo was built with a speaking timber from Dodona's oak, which is why the ship can speak.
"Doughty" means brave and strong; here it is used with some irony, since his courage is really bullying.
"Victuals" (pronounced "vittles") means food; "viands" in sentence 112 is a similar word.
The fate is a riddle: the sons of Boreas die if they fail to catch a fugitive, which explains why they later turn back.
The name Strophades comes from Greek strephein, "to turn"; the text gives this as the origin, through the verb estraphe.
Apollonius of Rhodes wrote the epic Argonautica, whose version of the Harpies' fate differs from the one just given.
"Thread the narrows" means steer carefully through the tight gap, like passing a thread through a needle.
The poop is the raised stern of the ship; its ornamented end was sheared off by the rocks.
The Thermodon is a river on the southern Black Sea coast, associated with the Amazons; the Caucasus is the mountain range at the eastern end of the Black Sea.
"Brazen-footed" means with feet of bronze; brazen here is literal, not 'shameless'.
Cadmus, founder of Thebes, sowed dragon's teeth that grew into armed men. Athena had given Aeetes half of the teeth.
"To have her to wife" means to take her as his wife.
"A knot of them" means a cluster or group of the armed men.
"He was taken to kill them" is odd; it means he was to set about killing them.
Tomi (on the Black Sea coast) is explained by Greek tomos, 'piece' or 'cut'; the name is said to commemorate the dismembered body.
"Divers" means various or several; "in divers places" means in many different places.
The Argo's timbers included a speaking beam from Dodona's oak, so the ship itself can prophesy. Ausonia is an old name for Italy.
The Sirens were creatures whose singing lured sailors to destruction; Orpheus's music was meant to drown out their song.
Scylla and Charybdis were a sea monster and a whirlpool flanking a narrow strait. The Wandering Rocks were moving cliffs that threatened ships.
"Kine" is an archaic plural of cow; the Sun's cattle were sacred herds.
"Maid" means virgin; Alcinous rules that a married Medea stays with Jason, an unmarried one returns to her father.
"Betook them" means "went"; "jested" refers to ritual banter at the sacrifice, which the text says became a custom.
A "vein" here is the single channel of his lifeblood, sealed by the nail.
Ichor is the fluid that flows in the veins of gods, here Talos's life-liquid.
Drinking bull's blood was traditionally believed to be fatal poison in Greek legend, which is how Aeson 'takes his own life' under the guise of sacrifice.
The Isthmus is the Isthmus of Corinth, where the Argo was dedicated to Poseidon, god of the sea, in thanks for the voyage.
'Make mince meat of' means to cut into small pieces; here it describes the daughters dismembering their father at Medea's instruction.
'The gods by whom Jason had sworn' refers to the oaths of fidelity Jason made to Medea; she calls on those gods to punish his breach.
'Suppliants' are people seeking protection by sitting at an altar; harming them was a grave religious offence.
'Deposed' means removed from power; Perses had overthrown his brother Aeetes, Medea's father.

context_notes.text: Delphi was the sanctuary of Apollo, where a priestess gave oracles that Greeks consulted on public crises.
Colchis lay at the eastern end of the Black Sea. Aeetes later guards the fleece against Jason and the Argonauts.
Hera punished Athamas and Ino because Ino had nursed the infant Dionysus, child of Zeus and Semele, Hera's rival.
Bellerophon, riding the winged horse Pegasus, killed the Chimera, a monster part lion, goat and serpent.
Asopus was a river god; Aegina was his daughter, and the island Aegina was later named for her.
Zeus's thunderbolt was his chief weapon; destroying Salmoneus and his city shows divine punishment for mortals claiming godhood.
Poseidon is the god of the sea, earthquakes and horses; he often takes human or other forms to seduce mortal women.
Pylus was Nestor's kingdom in the southwestern Peloponnese; Nestor later appears as the aged counsellor in the Iliad.
Hercules' attack on Pylus is usually told as vengeance after Neleus refused to purify him of a killing.
Pelias later sends Jason for the Golden Fleece, hoping he will die, and Alcestis is the wife who famously dies for her husband Admetus.
Bias is the brother of Melampus, the seer who understands animal speech; Pero's father Neleus is king of Pylus.
Dionysus is the god of wine; the madness of the Argive women was a punishment for resisting his worship.
The Epigoni were the sons of the Seven who died attacking Thebes; they later captured the city.
Artemis was goddess of wild animals and the hunt, and slighting her by omitting a sacrifice brought retribution.
The Fates were the goddesses who controlled the span of each mortal's life.
Colchis lay at the eastern end of the Black Sea. The Golden Fleece came from the ram that carried Phrixus there.
This catalogue of Argonauts gathers many famous heroes, including Hercules, Orpheus, Theseus and Atalanta, and shows the expedition's prestige.
Aphrodite is the goddess of love; neglecting her honors typically brings divine punishment in Greek myth.
The Doliones lived on the Propontis coast of Asia Minor, near Mysia.
Omphale was a Lydian queen whom Hercules served as a slave, as penance for a killing.
Boxing in the ancient world was brutal and could be fatal; Amycus forces visitors into matches they cannot win.
Pollux, a son of Zeus (Jove) and twin of Castor, was famed as a boxer among the Argonauts.
Harpies were storm-spirits, often depicted as winged women, who snatched food and people away.
Zetes and Calais, sons of the north wind Boreas, were winged Argonauts, so they could chase the flying Harpies.
Hera favored the Argonauts and helped Jason's expedition throughout the voyage.
Pelias, king of Iolcus, sent Jason for the fleece, hoping he would die, so that Jason would not claim the throne.
Hephaestus was the god of fire and metalworking, so fire-breathing bronze-footed bulls are fitting as his gift.
Medea is a sorceress. Her grandfather Ocean was the great river thought to encircle the world.
Zeus guarded oaths and the rights of kin and suppliants, so the murder of Apsyrtus, a kinsman, angered him.
Orpheus, the legendary musician, sailed with the Argonauts.
Thetis was a sea nymph, one of the Nereids, daughters of the sea god Nereus. Hera favored Jason's quest.
Hephaestus was the smith god; Minos was the legendary king of Crete. Talos was a bronze guardian of the island.
Iolcus was Jason's home city, where Pelias held the throne and had sent him for the Golden Fleece.
Jason's mother is Alcimede in other accounts; Pelias, who had usurped the throne of Iolcus, was Jason's uncle and enemy.
The fleece is the Golden Fleece, which Pelias had demanded Jason fetch from Colchis.
Corinth was the city where Jason and Medea settled; Creon was its king.
The Sun (Helios) was Medea's grandfather, which is why he could supply her with a chariot.
Aegeus was king of Athens and father of Theseus, which explains Medea's later plot against Theseus.

literary_notes.text: A false oracle is used to condemn an innocent child; religious authority becomes a tool of a stepmother's malice.
A divine mother intervenes at the last moment with a miraculous flying ram, rescuing the children from the altar.
Athamas loses the children of Ino through madness, a punishment mirroring his earlier near-sacrifice of Phrixus.
The endlessly rebounding stone symbolizes futile, repetitive labor as fitting punishment for Sisyphus's deceit.
Salmoneus's imitation of thunder with kettles and torches is a crude, almost comic parody, making his claim to be Zeus absurd and his doom deserved.
The mark on the baby's face gives rise to the name Pelias, hinting that the boy's identity and fate are shaped by this chance event.
Periclymenus' shifts into lion, snake and bee show his gift vividly, but his death shows that even divine power cannot save him from Hercules.
The snakes' tongues cleansing the ears symbolize the opening of mystical perception, a gift won by Melampus' kindness to the young snakes.
Melampus the prisoner gains his freedom by overhearing the worms, creatures that seem insignificant.
The collapse of the cell proves his prophetic power and prepares Phylacus's decision to free him.
The refusal of Admetus's parents contrasts with Alcestis's willingness, showing her devotion.
The oracle's warning about the one-sandaled man sets up Jason's arrival and the later ruin of Pelias.
Jason's offhand answer seals his own fate: he unknowingly names the very task Pelias will set him, and the reader sees the trap.
The Argonauts kill the king who had welcomed them; the mistake, discovered only at daylight, turns hospitality into grief and mourning.
The search for Hylas costs the two seekers their place on the voyage, as the ship sails off without them.
The narrator closes by piling up conflicting sources, presenting myth as a contested tradition rather than one settled story.
The stench of the leftover food makes the torment of Phineus vivid and repellent.
Mist and crashing sound create a vivid sense of danger, and the inverted word order adds an epic tone.
The dove losing only its tail tip hints that the ship will also barely escape with minor damage.
The rocks' final stillness ends the episode by fulfilling fate, making the Argonauts' success a turning point.
Armed men springing from sown teeth and turning on one another echoes the myth of Cadmus and Thebes.
Aeetes had set the task as a condition, but once Jason fulfils it he breaks his promise and plots treachery.
Medea's ruthless act shows her willingness to sacrifice family for Jason, and the grim tactic of delaying her father is told without comment.
The ship speaks like a person, giving the divine verdict and showing the voyage is guided by the gods.
The compiler lists rival versions with "some say," a mythographer's style that presents variant traditions without choosing among them.
Medea promises rejuvenation but delivers death; the ram trick makes the daughters complicit in murdering their own father.
Jason's betrayal is repaid through the bride's poisoned robe; the gift destroys Glauce and Creon, who tries to save her.
The narrative explains the name Media as derived from Medus, tying the legend to a real region.
